chapters.title: The whole system
chapters.lead: An MRI scanner is three magnetic systems nested inside one another, plus the electronics and cooling that drive them.
chapters.body:
Main magnet B0 aligns protons RF coils tip and listen Gradient coils encode position Computer builds the image 

- **Magnet**: Superconducting coils make a strong, very uniform, static field. Clinical systems are usually 1.5 T or 3 T.

- **Gradients**: Three coils (X, Y, Z) add small field slopes, switched on and off thousands of times per scan.

- **RF**: Coils transmit radio pulses at the Larmor frequency and pick up the faint echo from the body.

- **Room**: The scanner sits in a copper or aluminium RF shield (Faraday cage). Everything that needs power enters through a filtered penetration panel.

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom. Use **Peel layers** and **Explode** on the left at any time. The quarter cut-out shows the layers in section.

chapters.title: Assembly, layer by layer
chapters.lead: Press **Build next layer** to assemble the scanner from the inside of the magnet outward, in the order a factory would.

chapters.title: The superconducting magnet
chapters.lead: The main field B0 comes from coils of niobium-titanium (NbTi) wire embedded in copper. Below about 9 K, NbTi has zero electrical resistance.
chapters.body:
- **Persistent mode**: Once the magnet is ramped up, a superconducting switch closes the circuit. The current keeps flowing with no power supply, so the field is **always on**.

- **Six main coils**: Several coils along the axis, larger at the ends, shape the field so it is uniform over the imaging volume at the centre.

- **Shield coils**: Outer coils carry current in the opposite direction. They cancel much of the stray field outside, so the magnet needs less floor space.

- **Stored energy**: A clinical magnet stores megajoules of energy in its field.

Stray field Actively shielded Unshielded 
Larmor frequency Field vs Earth
chapters.safety: **Safety link.** The field does not switch off with the scanner. That is why the projectile risk in Zone IV exists day and night.

chapters.title: Cryostat and liquid helium
chapters.lead: The coils sit in liquid helium at 4.2 K (−269 °C) inside a cryostat built like a set of nested vacuum flasks.
chapters.body:
- **Helium vessel**: Holds the coils immersed in liquid helium.

- **Thermal shield**: An aluminium shell at roughly 40–50 K intercepts heat radiating inward.

- **Vacuum vessel**: The outer stainless shell at room temperature. The vacuum between the layers stops heat moving by conduction and convection.

- **Cold head**: A cryocooler on top, driven by a helium compressor, cools the shield and re-condenses evaporated helium. Many magnets now lose almost no helium in normal use.

- **Helium amount**: Older magnets hold well over a thousand litres. Some newer sealed designs need only a few litres.

Peel the outer layers with the slider to see each shell in turn.

chapters.title: Shimming the field
chapters.lead: A freshly built magnet is not uniform enough to image with. Shimming corrects it until the field varies by only a few parts per million across the imaging volume.
chapters.body:
- **Passive shims**: Small iron pieces placed in trays around the bore at installation, after the field is mapped.

- **Active shims**: Extra coils whose currents are adjusted for each patient, because the body itself distorts the field.

- **Why it matters**: Non-uniform field shifts frequencies, which shows up as distortion, signal loss and failed fat suppression.

Field variation over the sphere hundreds of ppm Colour green = on target 
Map and numbers are illustrative orders of magnitude, not measurements.

chapters.title: Gradient coils
chapters.lead: Three coils wound on a resin cylinder add a field that changes linearly along X, Y or Z. That slope is how the scanner knows where a signal came from.
chapters.body:
X saddle coils Y saddle coils Z Maxwell pairs 

Strength 
Field change across 40 cm Frequency spread 

- **Strength**: Clinical gradients reach tens of mT/m and switch at slew rates of the order of 100–200 T/m/s.

- **Noise**: Current pulses in the static field create Lorentz forces on the windings. The coil vibrates, which is the loud knocking. Patients need hearing protection.

- **Heat**: Gradient coils are water-cooled. Fast switching can also stimulate peripheral nerves, which limits how fast they are driven.

chapters.title: RF coils and the Faraday cage
chapters.lead: The body coil, a "birdcage" of copper rungs between two end rings, transmits a radio-frequency field B1 that rotates at the Larmor frequency. Smaller coils close to the body receive the echo.
chapters.body:
Transmit frequency Received signal**microvolts** 

- **Birdcage**: Currents in the rungs follow a sine pattern around the cage. The pattern rotates, producing a rotating B1 field in the bore.

- **Receive arrays**: Many small coil elements near the anatomy. Each picks up signal from a nearby region, which improves signal-to-noise and allows parallel imaging.

- **Shielding**: The room's RF shield keeps radio stations and electronics out of the tiny received signal, and keeps the scanner's pulses in.

- **Heating**: RF energy is absorbed by the body (specific absorption rate, SAR), so the scanner limits RF power.
chapters.safety: **Safety link.** Conductive loops (crossed legs, cables) can concentrate RF currents and cause burns. This is why positioning and cable routing are checked.

chapters.title: Protons in the field
chapters.lead: Hydrogen nuclei (protons) in water and fat behave like tiny magnets. In the field B0 they line up slightly more with the field than against it, and precess around it.
chapters.body:
f = γ̄ · B0    γ̄ = 42.58 MHz/T (hydrogen) 
B0 Precession frequency 

- **Net M**: The tiny excess aligned with B0 adds up to a net magnetisation M along the bore axis. MRI measures M, not single protons.

- **Real excess**: Only a few protons per million are in excess at clinical field strengths. The animation exaggerates it so you can see it.

- **Precession**: Shown slowed down by roughly a hundred million times.

chapters.title: RF excitation and the signal
chapters.lead: An RF pulse at the Larmor frequency tips M away from B0. The tipped magnetisation precesses and induces a voltage in the receive coil: the MR signal.
chapters.body:
Mz (along B0) 1.00 Mxy (transverse) 0.00 

- **Lab frame**: M spirals down as it is tipped and spirals back up as it relaxes, while precessing.

- **Rotating frame**: Viewed from a frame turning at the Larmor frequency, the precession disappears and the tip is a simple rotation about B1.

- **FID**: The decaying oscillation picked up after the pulse is the free induction decay.

chapters.title: Relaxation and contrast
chapters.lead: After the pulse, each tissue recovers at its own pace. T1 is regrowth along B0; T2 is loss of the transverse signal. Choosing TR and TE decides which difference shows up as brightness.
chapters.body:
TR (repetition time) 
TE (echo time) 
S = PD · (1 − e −TR/T1 ) · e −TE/T2 

SYNTHETIC HEAD · THIS TR/TE 

T1/T2 values are approximate 1.5 T figures for teaching; published values vary. The image is a synthetic phantom computed from the signal equation, not a scan.

chapters.title: Slice selection
chapters.lead: With the Z gradient on, every position along the bore has a slightly different Larmor frequency. An RF pulse containing only a narrow band of frequencies excites only the matching slice.
chapters.body:
The slab is drawn 10× thicker than the computed value so it is visible. 

- **Thinner slice**: Use a stronger gradient or a narrower RF bandwidth.

- **Move the slice**: Shift the RF centre frequency; the gradient stays the same.

chapters.title: From k-space to image
chapters.lead: Within the slice, the X and Y gradients give each location its own frequency and phase. Each repetition records one line of spatial frequencies (k-space). An inverse Fourier transform turns the filled k-space into the image.
chapters.body:
K-SPACE · 0 /128 LINES 
IMAGE · INVERSE FFT 
Keep only All lines Centre Edges 

- **Centre of k-space**: Low spatial frequencies: overall brightness and contrast. Keep only the centre and the image is blurred but the contrast is right.

- **Edges**: High spatial frequencies: fine detail and edges.

- **Scan time**: Roughly TR × number of phase-encode lines (× averages), which is why long-TR scans take minutes.

This runs a real 2D FFT on a synthetic phantom. Real scanners also correct for coil sensitivity, noise and motion.

chapters.title: Quench
chapters.lead: A quench is a sudden loss of superconductivity. The coil becomes resistive, the stored energy turns to heat, and the liquid helium boils off very quickly.
chapters.body:
- **Expansion**: Liquid helium expands roughly 750 times when it warms to room-temperature gas. The quench pipe carries it outside the building.

- **Hazards**: If gas enters the room: oxygen displacement, extreme cold, and pressure that can make an inward-opening door hard to open. Oxygen monitors and room ventilation help.

- **Magnet stop**: The magnet stop (emergency run-down) button deliberately quenches the magnet. It is for emergencies such as a person pinned by a ferromagnetic object. It is not the same as the emergency power-off.

- **Cost**: Re-filling helium and ramping the magnet back up takes days and is expensive.

Timescale is sped up. The animation is illustrative.
